title: Earth's whole history in one day
hook: Squeeze 4.54 billion years into 24 hours. How late in the day do we turn up?

knows: Earth is very old and humans came late
doesNotKnow: how late: the last few seconds of a day
that this scale is what lets slow processes (erosion, uplift, evolution) do large things

misconception: Humans have been around for a meaningful part of Earth's history.
objective: The learner can place our species in the last few seconds of a one-day clock of Earth's history (one clock second is about 52,500 years), and can say that the clock shows how long things took, not how fast they happened.

claims.text: On this clock 1 hour is about 189 million years, 1 minute about 3 million years and 1 second about 52,500 years.
claims.source: 4.54e9 / 24 = 189.2 million; / 1,440 = 3.15 million; / 86,400 = 52,546. Node, 2026-10-14. v2: the reveal quotes '1 second is about 52,500 years', the same figure as the stage caption in the last-minute view.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Node: 4.54e9 / 24 = 189.17 million (stage '1 hour ≈ 189 million years'); / 1,440 = 3.153 million ('1 minute ≈ 3 million years'); / 86,400 = 52,546 ('1 second ≈ 52,500 years'; the reveal says 'about 52,500'). The recall's 3.15 million mm = 3.15 km also re-checked.

claims.text: Where it stops: the clock shows how long things took, not how fast they happened; an even spread of time can hide sudden events.
claims.source: A linear clock maps duration only; it says nothing about rates within an interval (derivation). v2 (W-635): the example (the end-Cretaceous impact, c3) left the reveal so the limit rests on no held citation.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Derivation: the clock maps years ago to seconds linearly (Demo.tsx at()), so it encodes only when and how long; within any interval it carries no information about the rate of change, so a sudden event and a slow one over the same span look alike. Rests on no held citation.

claims.text: The Colorado River cut through the Grand Canyon about 6-5 million years ago; the canyon is about 1.8 km deep; how old its deepest parts are is debated. On the clock 6 million years ago is 23:58:05 and 5 million is 23:58:24.8, both at 23:58, in the last two minutes (stage dot at 6 million years, list: '23:58:05 Colorado River through Grand Canyon'; reveal: 'at 23:58, 6–5 million years ago, the Colorado River cut through the Grand Canyon, about 1.8 km deep. The age of its deepest parts is debated.').
claims.source: Timing: Nat Commun 2026 17: 8812, 'Tectonically driven integration of the 4.8 Ma Colorado River USA' (PMC13498593): 'river integration through the Grand Canyon 6-5 Ma'; the same paper reports paleocanyons cut across the Kaibab uplift before 15 Ma (older parts). Depth: PNAS 2025 (PMC12130896): Hells Canyon '~2,400 m deep' and '600 m deeper than the Grand Canyon', so about 1,800 m; the same paper calls the Grand Canyon's age 'controversial'. Nat Commun 2022 13: 4437 (PMC9343645), citing Karlstrom et al. (2014), 'Formation of the Grand Canyon 5 to 6 million years ago through integration of older palaeocanyons'. Sources as opened and quoted by fact-checker Pass 42; not opened by the builder. Clock (builder node, 2026-10-15): 86,400 - 6e6/4.54e9 x 86,400 = 86,285.8 s = 23:58:05; 86,400 - 5e6/4.54e9 x 86,400 = 86,304.8 s = 23:58:24.8. | Before the 2026-10-15 W-956 rewording: US National Park Service Grand Canyon geology pages; Karlstrom et al. (2008), Geology 36(11): 835-838 (rate 0.3 mm a year and 'most of the canyon' wording, now removed).
claims.note: Added by demo-builder (W-839, 2026-10-14); needs the fact-checker. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): UNVERIFIED. HELD, narrowed. Opened on PMC: Nat Commun 2026 17: 8812, 'Tectonically driven integration of the 4.8 Ma Colorado River USA' (PMC13498593): the proto-Colorado River was integrated 'between ~8 and 4.8 Ma', with an 'initial 6–5 Ma integration pathway', and 'the Marble Canyon segment of Grand Canyon ... was incised after 5 Ma'. It also discusses the competing 'paleocanyon solution'. Nat Commun 2022 13: 4437 (PMC9343645) cites Karlstrom et al. 2014, 'Formation of the Grand Canyon 5 to 6 million years ago through integration of older palaeocanyons', and describes older paleo-drainages later captured near 6 Ma. PNAS 2025 (PMC12130896) calls the Grand Canyon's age 'controversial'. So the timing 'in roughly the last 6 million years' is supported for the river's path through the canyon. 'Most' of the canyon is not quantified in what I opened (the 2014 title says older palaeocanyons were integrated), and the age is debated, as the claim's source field says. Not supported by any opened source: the depth '1.8 km', on which the reveal's '0.3 mm a year' rests (the NPS geology pages are not allow-listed). Fix: open an NPS or USGS page for the depth, or the builder words the reveal without the depth and rate (e.g. 'the Colorado River carved most of the Grand Canyon in the last two minutes on this clock, about 6 million years'). | FC pass 42 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): UNVERIFIED. HELD, narrowed again. Clock arithmetic re-run: 86,400 − 6e6/4.54e9 × 86,400 = 86,285.8 s = 23:58:05 (114 s before midnight); 1.8 km / 6 Myr = 0.30 mm a year. The depth is now sourced: PNAS 2025 (PMC12130896, opened) gives Hells Canyon '~2,400 m deep' and '600 m deeper than the Grand Canyon', so the Grand Canyon is about 1,800 m. Timing, opened: Nat Commun 2026 (PMC13498593) 'river integration through the Grand Canyon 6–5 Ma'. But the same paper says thermochronologic studies suggest 'paleocanyons had already been cut across the Kaibab uplift before 15 Ma', and the Marble Canyon segment 'was incised after 5 Ma'. Nat Commun 2022 (PMC9343645): the modern Colorado River 'would connect several old pre-existing segments of the Grand Canyon', citing Karlstrom et al. 2014, 'Formation of the Grand Canyon 5 to 6 million years ago through integration of older palaeocanyons'. PNAS 2025 calls the age 'controversial'. So the learner text 'carved the Grand Canyon's 1.8 km in the last two minutes', with its 0.3 mm/yr rate, assumes the whole depth is younger than 6 Myr, and the opened sources say parts are older. 'Most' (claim text) is not quantified in anything I opened. Fix (demo-builder; cm-big-ideas wording): drop the rate and the whole-depth claim, e.g. stage 'Colorado River through Grand Canyon' and reveal 'the Colorado River joined older canyons into the 1.8 km-deep Grand Canyon in the last two minutes (about 6 million years)', citing PMC13498593 and PMC12130896. Or open Karlstrom 2014 and quote how much of the depth is younger than 6 Ma. | Reset to unverified by demo-builder (2026-10-15): W-956 (FC42): rate (0.3 mm a year) and the whole-depth claim ('carved the Grand Canyon's 1.8 km in the last two minutes', 'most of') removed from the stage, reveal and claim. Kept only what Pass 42 found sourced (river through the canyon about 6-5 Ma; depth about 1.8 km) plus a plain statement that the age of the deepest parts is debated. Stage label 'Grand Canyon carved, 1.8 km' -> 'Colorado River through Grand Canyon'. | FC pass 44 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15, W-963): DISPUTED (wording; the sourced facts hold). I opened all three sources myself as full text from the PMC OAI service (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/api/oai; the article pages returned reCAPTCHA). They say what the source field quotes. PMC13498593: 'river integration through the Grand Canyon 6–5 Ma' and 'integration of the upper and lower Colorado basins through Grand Canyon at 5.1 Ma'. The same paper: 'paleocanyons had already been cut across the Kaibab uplift before 15 Ma', 'the Marble Canyon segment of Grand Canyon ... was incised after 5 Ma', and the ≤4.6-4.3 Ma Bullhead Alluvium 'records active incision of Grand Canyon'. PMC12130896: Hells Canyon '~2,400 m deep', '600 m deeper than the Grand Canyon' (so about 1,800 m), and the Grand Canyon is one of the 'controversial places'. PMC9343645: the modern river 'would connect several old pre-existing segments of the Grand Canyon', citing Karlstrom 2014. Clock (node, own copy): 6 Ma = 86,285.8 s = 23:58:05; 5 Ma = 86,304.8 s = 23:58:24.8. Both are 23:58, so the stage dot and list line are fine. The problem is the reveal sentence as a learner reads it: 'Given this much time, even a process too slow to see can do large things: at 23:58, 6–5 million years ago, the Colorado River cut through the Grand Canyon, about 1.8 km deep.' The colon presents this as the large thing the slow process did. 'Cut through ... about 1.8 km deep' then reads most naturally as 'cut 1.8 km down at 23:58', which implies about 1.8 mm a year over 1 Myr. The opened sources contradict that: parts were cut before 15 Ma, and incision went on after 5 Ma. The hedge does not fix this. 'The age of its deepest parts is debated' is in none of the opened sources. They debate the age of older segments along the canyon (paleocanyons), not its deepest parts. At any one place a canyon cuts downward, so its deepest rock is the most recently cut, and the hedge points the learner the wrong way. Fix (demo-builder; cm-big-ideas wording), e.g.: 'at 23:58, 6–5 million years ago, the Colorado River joined older stretches of canyon into one path through what is now the 1.8 km-deep Grand Canyon. How old those stretches are is debated.' Every part of that wording is in PMC13498593, PMC9343645 and PMC12130896 as opened. Then update the claim text to match. Whether the example still shows 'large things' is for cm-big-ideas, not me (pedagogy). The walkthrough transcript and screenshots are from 2026-10-14, before v4, so I read the v4 text from Demo.tsx. | Withdrawn by cm-big-ideas ruling W-979 (company/reviews/earth-history-in-a-day/2026-10-15-cm-ruling.md): the Grand Canyon example leaves the stage and the reveal. Pass 44's wording was accurate but no longer showed a slow process doing a large thing in the time shown, and a second held sentence in the reveal breaks big-ideas-strategy D4(b).

recall.question: A river cuts 1 mm deeper each year. On the one-day clock of Earth's history, how deep does it cut in the last minute?
recall.why: One clock minute is about 3.15 million years (4.54 billion ÷ 1,440). At 1 mm a year that is about 3.15 million mm, about 3 km: slow processes do large things given deep time.
